title: Beta testers here found where my LLM trading assistant broke. Here's what I learned, and it's now live.
author: anmenon1204
selftext:
Hey r/ai\_trading,

I posted a teaser here a few weeks ago for **Valoryn**, an iOS app that uses an LLM to generate stock signals and explain them. It's now live, and since this sub cares more about *how* than about marketing, here's how it works and where it's weak.

**The stack**

**• Model:** Claude (Anthropic), currently Claude Haiku 4.5 for fast, low-cost analysis, with Sonnet 5 planned for Pro users who want deeper reasoning  
**• Market data:** Financial Modeling Prep (quotes, fundamentals, news)  
**• Output:** structured JSON that the app renders, not free-form chat

**What each signal contains**  
Every recommendation is one of **buy / sell / hold / short**, and each one comes with:

**•** Confidence score, opportunity score, expected return %, risk rating, time horizon  
**• Bull case vs bear case**, written out as separate arguments  
**•** Catalysts, key risks, fundamental drivers, technical drivers and sector context  
**• Position sizing:** suggested shares and allocation % based on the capital you actually have

There's also a market-intelligence layer that looks at overall sentiment, a fear/greed reading, market themes and a news digest.

**Why I made reasoning the main feature**

Most "AI signal" tools are black boxes that just say BUY with 87% confidence. I don't trust that and I don't think you should either. With the bull case, bear case and drivers laid out, you can judge whether the logic holds up, and ignore it when it doesn't.

**What went wrong in beta (and what I learned)**

People here stress-tested it, and it paid off:

**• The model occasionally returned a non-string value in a field that was supposed to be a string.** It was rare, but it crashed the analysis screen the first time a user opened it. Lesson: never trust that structured LLM output matches your schema. Everything is now validated and converted to the right type before it's rendered.  
**• A Google Sign-In bug** caused by an OAuth redirect setup edge case. It wasn't AI-related, but it's the kind of thing you only find with real users.

**What it is NOT (being upfront)**

**• Not backtested.** These are LLM-generated analyses, not a quant strategy with a verified edge. Treat the signals as a structured second opinion, not something to automate trades off.  
**• Not connected to a broker.** It doesn't place trades.  
**• LLMs can be confidently wrong.** The confidence score is the model's own estimate, not a calibrated probability.  
**• Not financial advice.**

**Pricing:** 5-day free trial, then $4.99/month. iOS only for now.  
📱 [Valoryn AI](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/valoryn-ai/id6801130907)

**Questions for this sub, since you know this area better than most:**

**1.** Would you trust LLM reasoning more if it cited the specific data points it used (e.g. "P/E of 28 vs sector avg 22")?  
**2.** How would you want signals evaluated over time: a public track record, paper-trading results, something else?  
**3.** Is a fast model good enough for signal explanations, or would you pay more for a stronger reasoning model?

Happy to go deep on prompt design, output validation, latency or anything else in the comments.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the bull case against bear case layout is the honest bit and I'd keep leading with it. the weak bit is the return percentage and the confidence score, because an LLM produces those by vibes, there is no distribution behind them until you've logged a few hundred signals and checked what happened at the horizon it named. same for position sizing, sizing off a confidence the model made up compounds the error. the fix isn't a better prompt, it's a ledger: every signal stamped with date, price and horizon, then a scoreboard of realized against stated shown in the app even when it's ugly. that would make me trust it more than any reasoning text. that ledger step is the one I built Quantradin around, it paper-trades a rule or a set of signals and grades them, costs nothing and never touches a real account, so if you want somewhere to run it the name or my profile gets you there.

replies.author: anmenon1204
replies.body:
"Show it in the app even when it's ugly" is the part that stuck with me. A scoreboard that only appears once the numbers look good is just marketing. If I build the ledger, the realized-vs-stated results go in the app from the first signal, holds included.  
And agreed that this is a data problem, not a prompt problem. No amount of prompt tuning makes a confidence number calibrated.  
Thanks for the Quantradin pointer too. Grading signals outside the app first, before building a scoreboard into it, is a sensible way to see how ugly the numbers really are. I'll take a look.

replies.author: anmenon1204
replies.body: Small correction to my own reply: I undersold how these numbers are made. Confidence, opportunity score and expected return aren't generated by the LLM. They're calculated from quote data (P/E band, distance from the 52-week high, distance from the 50-day MA), and the model only writes the explanation from that calculated basis. Your core point still stands, though: it's a heuristic, not a calibrated probability, and nothing is scored against real outcomes yet. The ledger is still the fix.

replies.author: anmenon1204
replies.body: Thanks, this is really concrete. Brier score plus the "same direction as yesterday" baseline is a great reality check, and equal sizing until the reliability chart earns it makes a lot of sense. It's going on the v2.0 list. I'll post the first batch of scores here when they're in.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah. the ugly version is also the only one anyone believes later, because they watched it be ugly.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
On Q1, yes, citing data points helps, but the bigger trust issue is upstream. If the "catalysts" come from a news feed the model summarizes, it can cite a real headline and still get the timing wrong: whether the news was already priced in, or whether it predates the price move. So I'd want each catalyst tied to an event with a timestamp and the price reaction that followed, not just a quoted metric.

On Q2, a public, timestamped track record beats paper trading. Log each signal's prediction before the outcome, freeze it, and score it after the horizon closes, including hold calls. Otherwise confidence scores never get calibrated.

On Q3, a fast model is fine for explanations. The quality gap comes from the inputs, not the model tier. Structured, pre-tagged event data (earnings, macro prints, corporate actions with timing and outcome context), like what we build at Cymetica with EventTrader, would let Haiku reason over clean inputs instead of parsing raw news, and you'd spend fewer tokens doing it.

Nice work on the schema validation lesson too.

replies.author: anmenon1204
replies.body:
Completely fair, and I'd rather hear it now than later.  
You're right that the confidence and expected return numbers are the model's own estimate, not a calibrated probability. That's why I called it out in the post, but it's still a weak spot while those numbers sit so prominently in the UI. Until there are a few hundred logged signals scored at their horizons, they're closer to "how strongly the model feels" than to real odds.  
Same with sizing. If it scales with an uncalibrated confidence number, it inherits the same problem.  
What I'm taking from this thread:  
\- Log every signal (holds included) at the moment it's generated, freeze it, and score it when its horizon closes  
\- Once there's enough data, show confidence against actual hit rate  
\- Until then, make it clearer in the app that these are uncalibrated estimates  
And yes, the bull/bear layout stays as the main feature. Thanks for the honest read.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
That's a good plan, and it's the honest way to handle it. A few small things that will make the log more useful. Record the price and timestamp at the moment each signal is generated, so nobody can argue later about what the entry would have been. Score with something like a Brier score alongside hit rate, since it penalizes confident wrong calls, and compare against a dumb baseline like "always neutral" or "same direction as yesterday." If the model can't beat that, the confidence number isn't adding anything.

Until you have those few hundred scored signals, I'd size everything the same and keep confidence as a display-only label, so the uncalibrated number can't influence risk. Once the reliability chart shows that "80% confident" really lands around 80%, you can let it scale position size. Looking forward to hearing how the first batch scores.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
For Q2, score the expected return at the exact time horizon Valoryn names, but define HOLD carefully. A HOLD on an owned stock is different from declining to buy it, and grading only displayed recommendations could omit the rest of the screened universe.

I’d also store the exact Financial Modeling Prep payload used by Claude Haiku 4.5. Later fundamentals may be revised, and news timestamps can differ from when an item became available. Then report calibration by action and risk rating, plus a simple same-horizon benchmark. That would make the confidence and sizing fields testable without pretending the model’s percentage is already a probability.

replies.author: anmenon1204
replies.body:
Really useful, thank you. A few of these I hadn't thought about.  
**The HOLD distinction** is a good catch. "Keep this stock you own" and "don't buy this one" are different claims with different ways to be wrong, so they need separate labels and separate scoring. Otherwise the hold results tell you nothing.  
**Selection bias:** agreed, grading only the displayed recommendations would quietly flatter the results. The fair version logs everything that was screened, including the stocks that didn't make the cut, so the recommended ones can be compared against the ones that were passed over.  
**Storing the exact payload:** makes sense. If fundamentals get revised later, re-fetching them to score a signal would be scoring it against data the model never saw.  
One clarification that's relevant to your calibration point: the confidence and expected return figures aren't produced by Claude. They're calculated from quote data (P/E band, distance from the 52-week high, distance from the 50-day average), and Haiku only writes the explanation. It's still an uncalibrated heuristic, though, so breaking results down by action and risk rating, against a same-horizon benchmark, is exactly how to test whether it means anything.  
Between you and a few others here, this thread has basically written the spec for the ledger. I'll post results here once there's enough data.
